title: Given a Scenario, Troubleshoot Common Cabling and Physical Interface Issues

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Physical-layer failures often appear as intermittent links, poor performance, interface errors, or devices that never power on. Diagnose the medium, signal, termination, interface, power, and transceiver in a deliberate order.
bullets: Improper termination and reversed transmit/receive paths
Transceiver mismatches and weak optical signals
sections.callout: CHECK MEDIUM → CHECK SIGNAL → CHECK TERMINATION → CHECK INTERFACE → CHECK POWER → CHECK TRANSCEIVER

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Match the symptom to the physical component most capable of producing it.
bullets: Wrong medium or rating → Incorrect cable
Power demand exceeds available supply → PoE budget exceeded

entries.title: Single-Mode vs. Multimode Fiber
paragraphs: Single-mode fiber supports long distances with a small core and matched optics. Multimode fiber supports shorter links with a larger core. Mixing media or optics can prevent a stable link.
entries.memoryHook: Long distance → single-mode; shorter building links → multimode.

entries.title: Category 5/6/7/8
paragraphs: Copper category determines supported frequency, construction, distance, and performance. A lower category or poor installation can prevent the intended Ethernet speed.
entries.memoryHook: The link can only perform as well as its weakest cable segment.

entries.title: STP vs. UTP
paragraphs: Shielded twisted pair (STP) adds protection in electrically noisy environments but requires correct grounding. Unshielded twisted pair (UTP) is common and easier to install but offers less external-noise protection.

entries.title: Crosstalk
paragraphs: Signals from one wire pair interfere with another pair in the same or nearby cable.

entries.title: Interference
paragraphs: External electromagnetic or radio-frequency energy disrupts the signal. Motors, fluorescent lighting, power cabling, and radio transmitters are common sources.

entries.title: Attenuation
paragraphs: Signal strength decreases as distance increases or as connectors and splices add loss.
entries.memoryHook: The signal fades along the path.

entries.title: Improper Termination
paragraphs: Wrong pinouts, loose conductors, excessive untwisting, contamination, or damaged connectors can create opens, shorts, intermittent links, and performance loss.
entries.memoryHook: Inspect both ends and test the cable map.

entries.title: TX/RX Transposed
paragraphs: A transmitter (TX) must connect to the receiver (RX) on the opposite end. Reversed fiber strands or polarity prevent communication even when the components are otherwise correct.

entries.title: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC)
paragraphs: CRC errors indicate frames arrived corrupted, commonly because of bad cabling, interference, duplex issues, or failing interfaces.
entries.memoryHook: The frame arrived, but its integrity check failed.

entries.title: Runts
paragraphs: Runts are Ethernet frames smaller than the minimum valid frame size.

entries.title: Giants
paragraphs: Giants exceed the expected maximum frame size and can reflect MTU or framing problems.

entries.title: Drops
paragraphs: Drops show frames or packets discarded because of congestion, buffer limits, errors, or policy.

entries.title: Error Disabled
paragraphs: The switch automatically disabled the port after detecting a violation or fault such as port security, BPDU guard, or link instability.

entries.title: Administratively Down
paragraphs: An administrator intentionally disabled the interface in configuration.

entries.title: Suspended
paragraphs: The port is prevented from forwarding because of a logical consistency or bundling problem, often involving a link-aggregation group.
entries.memoryHook: Configuration inconsistency holds the port out.

entries.title: Power Budget Exceeded
paragraphs: The switch has insufficient remaining power for another powered device even though the port supports PoE.

entries.title: Incorrect Standard
paragraphs: The power sourcing equipment and powered device require compatible PoE standards and power levels. A lower standard may not provide enough wattage.

entries.title: Mismatch
paragraphs: Both ends must agree on medium, wavelength, speed, distance class, connector, and supported transceiver type.

entries.title: Signal Strength
paragraphs: Optical power that is too weak can result from distance, dirty connectors, excessive bends, bad splices, failing optics, or too many loss points.
entries.memoryHook: Inspect the optical budget and path.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Wrong fiber distance/type → Single-mode vs. multimode mismatch
Long run and weak signal → Attenuation
No remaining PoE capacity → Budget exceeded

entries.title: Crosstalk vs. Interference
paragraphs: Crosstalk comes from other signal pairs; interference comes from an external electromagnetic or radio source.

entries.title: Interference vs. Attenuation
paragraphs: Interference adds unwanted energy; attenuation is loss of signal strength over the path.

entries.title: CRC vs. Drops
paragraphs: CRC means corrupted frames were received; drops mean traffic was discarded.

entries.title: Runts vs. Giants
paragraphs: Runts are below the minimum frame size; giants exceed the maximum.

entries.title: Error Disabled vs. Administratively Down
paragraphs: Error disabled is an automatic protective response; administratively down is an intentional configuration state.

entries.title: PoE Budget vs. Standard
paragraphs: Budget describes total available power; standard describes compatible delivery capability.

entries.title: Transceiver Mismatch vs. Signal Strength
paragraphs: Mismatch means incompatible endpoints; signal strength means the selected link is suffering excessive optical loss.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
sections.callout: MEDIUM → SIGNAL → TERMINATION → INTERFACE → POWER → TRANSCEIVER
